title: Non-determinism, pass^k and significance
summary: Run each task several times. Report pass@k when one success is enough and pass^k when every run must succeed. Attach a confidence interval to every pass rate and compare versions paired, because small eval sets cannot see small differences.
useIf: An agent or prompt change moves a score by a few points and you must decide whether it is real.
avoidIf: The system is deterministic and fully checkable, where one run is the truth.

explain.md: Scores vary because sampling, tools, the environment and the judge are all noisy. So run each task n times. Two summaries answer different questions: **pass@k** is the chance at least one of k trials succeeds, and **pass^k** is the chance all k succeed. tau-bench defines pass^k and gives unbiased estimators from n trials with c successes per task, averaged over tasks [[r23]].

explain.title: Unbiased estimators (tau-bench)
explain.expr: pass^k = mean over tasks of C(c, k) / C(n, k);  pass@k = 1 - mean over tasks of C(n - c, k) / C(n, k)

vars.v: trials that must (pass^k) or may (pass@k) succeed

explain.example: Ten trials, seven successes, k = 3: pass^3 = C(7,3) / C(10,3) = 35 / 120 = 0.292. pass^1 equals pass@1 [[r23]].

explain.md: Reliability decays fast. If every trial succeeded with the same probability p, pass^k would be p^k. This is a computed estimate, because real tasks vary in difficulty.

In tau-bench, gpt-4o with function calling scored about 61% in retail and 35% in airline at pass^1, and about 25% in retail at pass^8 (2024 model) [[r23]]. Use pass@k when one success is enough, for example code the user can retry, and pass^k when consistency matters, such as a customer-facing agent [[r17]]. The gap can be large: the Codex paper's abstract reports 28.8% of problems solved with one sample and 70.2% with 100 samples per problem, and its Table 2 lists 72.3% at 100 samples for the 12B model [[tr8]].

explain.caption: 95% half-width for an 80% pass rate (computed: 1.96 x sqrt(p(1-p)/n) [[r24]])
head: Items n

explain.md: At n = 100, an 80% pass rate is anywhere from about 72% to 88%, so a 3-point gain is noise. Anthropic's error-bar guidance adds clustered standard errors when questions are grouped (they can exceed 3x the naive value), paired question-level differences when comparing two models, and power analysis [[r24]]. For small n or rates near 0 or 100%, the Wilson interval behaves better than the normal approximation, and the rule of three says zero failures in n runs bounds the failure rate near 3/n [[tr9]]. Foundry's compare view marks a change strong at p <= 0.001 and weak at 0.001 < p <= 0.05 [[r39]].

whereToUse: Customer-facing agents, where pass^k with k near the number of repeat uses matters
Code or search assistants, where pass@k shows the value of retry or best-of-n
Release gates that must say a change is real, not noise
Model upgrade decisions between two close candidates

use: A decision hinges on a few points
Reliability, not peak ability, is the requirement
avoid: Reporting one run of a stochastic agent as the score
Comparing two means without an interval or pairing
Computing p^k from an average p and calling it measured
flips: User can retry or pick the best: pass@k
Eval set under about 100 items: report intervals and treat small deltas as unproven
Gap target is small: size the set with a power analysis

pitfalls.symptom: A prompt tweak raised the score 2 points then lost it next run
pitfalls.cause: A single run on a small set, so the difference is inside the noise
pitfalls.fix: Repeat trials, report an interval and compare paired against the baseline

pitfalls.symptom: pass^5 is far lower than predicted from the mean pass rate
pitfalls.cause: Tasks differ in difficulty, so failures concentrate on some tasks
pitfalls.fix: Estimate pass^k per task from repeated trials, not as p^k

pitfalls.symptom: Many metrics, and some always regress
pitfalls.cause: More metrics mean more chances of a false alarm
pitfalls.fix: Name one or two primary metrics per gate and correct for multiple tests

scenarios.title: Refund agent, every call must be right
scenarios.situation: An agent processes customer refunds. A customer may interact with it several times a month. Each wrong refund costs money and trust. A 100-task eval is available and runs are affordable.
unknowns: How many repeat interactions per customer?
scenarios.question: How do you report the agent's reliability?

options.name: Run 8 trials per task, report pass^k for k near real repeat use, with an interval
options.why: Consistency is the product requirement, and pass^k exposes decay that a mean hides.
options.tradeoff: Eight times the runs and judge cost.

options.name: Report the mean pass rate from one run
options.why: It hides variance and makes a 75% agent look fine when three in a row succeed only about 42% of the time.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for a first rough screen.

options.name: Report pass@8
options.tradeoff: Overstates reliability when users cannot pick the best of eight.

flips.if: A human reviews every output and picks
Budget limits runs to 3 per task

scenarios.takeaway: Customer-facing reliability is a pass^k question.

scenarios.title: Two prompts, 40 items, a 3-point gap
scenarios.situation: A team compares two prompt versions on a 40-item set. Version B scores 3 points higher. Labelling more items is slow.
unknowns: Are the same items used for both?
scenarios.question: What do you conclude and do next?

options.name: Treat it as unproven, run repeated trials with a paired comparison and grow the set
options.why: At n=40 the interval is about plus or minus 12 points, so 3 points is noise. Pairing the same items cuts variance.

options.name: Ship B because it scored higher
options.why: The gap sits well inside the interval.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable if the change is free, reversible and harmless.

options.name: Compute a t-test on the single run and ship if p < 0.05
options.why: Better than nothing and gives a defensible number.
options.tradeoff: One noisy run on 40 items gives a fragile test.

flips.then: A 3-point gap becomes measurable but still needs pairing.

flips.if: B costs less and is not worse
flips.then: A non-inferiority framing may justify shipping.

scenarios.takeaway: Small sets cannot see small gaps.

quiz.q: A task is tried 10 times and succeeds 7 times. Using the unbiased estimator, what is pass^3 for this task? Give a decimal.
quiz.explain: C(7,3) = 35 and C(10,3) = 120, so 35 / 120 = 0.2917. That is far below the 0.7 per-trial rate.

quiz.q: An agent succeeds on each independent trial with probability 0.75. Roughly what is the chance of three successes in a row, in percent?
quiz.explain: 0.75^3 = 0.4219, about 42%. This assumes identical independent trials, which real tasks only approximate.

quiz.q: Which change makes pass@k the better headline metric than pass^k?
options: A user can retry or pick the best of several outputs
The eval set doubled in size
quiz.explain: pass@k credits at least one success, which matches workflows where retry or best-of-n exists. Tool use, set size and judge cost do not change which question you ask.

flashcards.back: pass@k: at least one of k trials succeeds. pass^k: all k trials succeed. pass^1 equals pass@1. Use pass^k when consistency matters.

flashcards.front: 95% half-width at n=100 for an 80% pass rate?
flashcards.back: About 7.8 points (1.96 x sqrt(0.8 x 0.2 / 100)). At n=400 it is 3.9 and at n=1,000 it is 2.5.
Question-level differences on the same items cancel item difficulty and shrink variance. Anthropic's error-bar guidance recommends it, plus clustered standard errors and power analysis.
